passage:
"Vandana, why are you taking that photo eleven times?" Madhuri asked from the bed.
"Because the first ten make my hair look flat. Hold on, I'm cropping out the dirty cups."
"There are dirty cups?"
"Exactly. Nobody needs to know." Vandana typed a caption, deleted it, typed another: "monday mood 🙂". Then she stuck a sleepy-cat meme in the corner.
"That's a happy caption on a tired face."
"It's a joke, didi. Everyone in my class posts the cat one. It means we all hate Mondays."
"So it says you're with them."
"Kind of." Vandana paused. "Honestly I had a rotten day. But that's not what this is for." She pressed post and put the phone face down.

qa.q: What did Vandana crop out of the photo?
qa.a: She cropped out the dirty cups.

qa.q: What might Vandana be feeling as she posts a cheerful caption?
qa.a: Most likely she is covering a rotten day with a joke, since she admits it aloud, though she may also just want to join her class's cat meme and feel she belongs.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say next to keep Vandana talking?
qa.a: She could ask about the rotten day without criticising the post, so Vandana can share the parts the photo left out. 🙂

qa.q: How does Madhuri's view of the post differ from her classmates' view?
qa.a: Madhuri saw the tired face and the tidying, so the caption looks mismatched to her, while classmates only see the finished cat meme and may read it as a shared Monday joke.

grounding: A teen frames and edits a photo and meme to signal belonging and mood, showing a presented self rather than the whole day.

passage: Last year I thought a good selfie needed twenty tries and three filters. My friend Tanuja and I had a private group where we posted only our funniest edits: Tanuja's face on a potato, my face on a sad monsoon crow. Those memes were the best part of my day, and we never shared the ordinary photos. Then Tanuja stayed at my place after a cousin's wedding and scrolled through my page. "You look like you're always at a party," she said. I laughed, but I looked at my grid afterwards and it did show a sparkling girl I didn't quite know. I still post memes. I just leave a few plain photos in too. - Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita and Tanuja post in their private group?
qa.a: They posted only their funniest edits, such as Tanuja's face on a potato and Nikita's face on a sad monsoon crow.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when she looked at her own grid after Tanuja's remark?
qa.a: She felt a little unsettled, since the grid showed a sparkling girl she didn't quite know, though she also laughed, so she may have taken the remark partly as a compliment.

qa.q: What small change did Nikita make, and why might it help?
qa.a: She added a few plain photos among the memes, which keeps the humour while showing more of her ordinary life.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have meant her comment?
qa.a: It could be admiration, or a gentle observation that the page shows only parties. Tanuja's own edits were chosen too, so she may be noticing something familiar. 🙂

grounding: A teen looks back on curating memes and selfies as a chosen, framed self that leaves out ordinary life.

passage: Aiko noticed the ticket stub the moment Felix opened his locker in the corridor of their Hamburg school. It was creased and taped at one corner, beside a photo of a train window. She almost said, "Ooh, whose concert was that, a date?" but Felix's shoulders had gone stiff, so she asked, "What's the story with that?" He touched the tape. "It's from the last match my grandfather took me to before he moved into the care home," he said. "The team lost. I don't even like football much." He shut the locker gently. "I just like seeing it when I'm stuck on maths." Aiko nodded. "Then it's a good place for it."

qa.q: Where was the ticket stub kept?
qa.a: It was taped inside Felix's locker, next to a photo of a train window.

qa.q: What might Felix be feeling about the ticket stub?
qa.a: Probably tenderness and some sadness about his grandfather; his stiff shoulders and gentle closing of the locker suggest it matters, though the stiffness could also be embarrassment at being asked.

qa.q: Why was asking about the story wiser than guessing?
qa.a: Aiko's guess of a date would have been wrong, and the question let Felix explain a meaning only he knew.

qa.q: How might Felix have reacted if Aiko had said her guess aloud?
qa.a: It could have felt like teasing about something tender, and he might have closed up instead of telling her about his grandfather.

grounding: A teen keeps a ticket stub whose meaning only he can explain, and a friend's curiosity beats assumption.

passage: In the chemistry lab, Farida Ma'am held up the rule sheet: no loose jewellery near the burners. Deepika looked at her wrist. The bracelet was faded green thread, knotted three times at the clasp, with one bead missing. "Ma'am, can I keep it in my pocket instead?" Her voice was quiet. The teacher could have said a rule is a rule, and it was. But Farida said, "Pocket is fine. Is it special?" Deepika slid it off slowly. "My best friend made it before she moved to another city. We each have one." "Then zip it inside your bag, away from the burners," said Farida. Deepika did, patting the zip twice before she picked up her test tube.

qa.q: What was the lab rule about?
qa.a: The rule was no loose jewellery near the burners.

qa.q: What does Deepika's slow removal of the bracelet suggest?
qa.a: She values it and is reluctant to part with it, probably because it links her to the friend who made it, though she may also just feel shy at being singled out.

qa.q: What can a teacher do when a safety rule meets a keepsake?
qa.a: Keep the rule but offer a safe alternative, like a zipped bag, and ask kindly about the object, so safety and the student's feelings are both respected.

qa.q: How might Farida see the moment differently from Deepika?
qa.a: For the teacher it is a safety rule with an easy fix, while for Deepika it is a link to a friend who moved away, so a cold enforcement would have felt like a loss.

grounding: A teen's friendship bracelet stands for a relationship only its owner can explain; the adult responds with curiosity.

passage: Every morning that month, Vinita reached the bus stop later than her friends. She had ironed her kurta twice with the heavy coal iron and tried her hair in three different partings. Since her cousin's phone had shown her the town girls' pictures, all smooth skin and glowing eyes, her own face in the steel mirror seemed wrong somehow. At Rafiq's tea stall she stood behind the sacks, checking her reflection in a glass jar. Rafiq, who had known her since she was small, set down a cup. "Beti, those pictures are polished by a machine before anyone sees them. Dress how it pleases you. That's your choice, it isn't what you're worth." She smiled, not fully believing him. "If it keeps sitting heavy on you," he added, "tell your mother or your teacher."

qa.q: How many times did Vinita iron her kurta?
qa.a: She ironed her kurta twice with the heavy coal iron.

qa.q: How might Vinita be feeling about her own face, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels unsure or dissatisfied, shown by the repeated ironing, the changed partings and the checking of her reflection; her half-believing smile suggests she is only partly reassured.

qa.q: What would help Vinita if the worry does not ease?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult such as her mother or her teacher, as Rafiq suggested, so that lasting distress gets caring attention.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq's words carry weight with Vinita?
qa.a: He has known her since she was small, so the comment comes from a familiar, caring adult and not from someone judging her looks.

grounding: A teen compares herself with filtered pictures and over-controls grooming; a supportive adult says presentation is a choice, not worth.

passage: The bus horn sounded outside the Manchester terrace, and Chidi was still pulling on his fourth shirt. Paulo waited on the step, hood up against the drizzle. "You looked fine three shirts ago." "You haven't seen what the older boys post," Chidi said, tugging at the collar. "Their arms, their skin, everything perfect." "They pick one out of forty and put it through a filter. My cousin does it." Paulo shrugged. "My mum says clothes are a choice, not a scoreboard." Chidi gave a short, stiff laugh and put the first shirt back on. On the bus Paulo sent a message: talk to me if it gets heavy, or to your form tutor.

qa.q: How many shirts had Chidi tried on when the horn sounded?
qa.a: He was pulling on his fourth shirt.

qa.q: What might Chidi be worried about when he compares himself with the older boys?
qa.a: He may be afraid that his own looks don't measure up to their perfect pictures; his stiff laugh suggests the comparison is bothering him more than he admits.

qa.q: What small step could help Chidi if the comparing continues?
qa.a: He could talk to Paulo or his form tutor, as Paulo suggested, and remember that the photos were picked and filtered.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel watching his friend change shirts again and again?
qa.a: He is probably concerned but trying to stay light, which is why he jokes first and then sends a quiet message offering to listen.

grounding: A teen over-controls clothes after comparing with filtered images, and a friend frames presentation as choice and offers support.

passage: "Jahnavi, can I ask something?" Rafiq said, walking beside her to school. "Sure." "Why do you always wear a dupatta? Does your family make you?" "Some days it's Amma's rule," Jahnavi said. "Some days it feels like me. Today it just matched my kurta." She grinned. "You're not the first to guess." "Sorry. I assumed." "Everyone does. My cousin wears hers for prayer, my friend Sana never wears one, and neither of us is wrong." "So you can't tell from looking." "Exactly. You'd have to ask, and listen." Rafiq laughed, embarrassed. "Okay. I'm listening. 😅"

qa.q: Who asked Jahnavi about the dupatta?
qa.a: Rafiq asked her, while they were walking to school.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling after Jahnavi answered?
qa.a: He felt a little embarrassed and sorry for assuming, as his apology and laugh show, and probably some curiosity too. 😅

qa.q: How could Rafiq ask about someone's clothing without assuming?
qa.a: He could ask an open, friendly question and really listen, accepting that the same item can be faith, family expectation, choice or style.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when people guess about her dupatta?
qa.a: Somewhat tired of being assumed about, as 'Everyone does' hints, yet she stays friendly and explains patiently.

grounding: A teenager's dupatta can mean family rule, personal feeling or style, so others should ask rather than assume.

passage: After my thread ceremony I thought I'd feel different. Mostly I felt itchy. In the changing room before PE a boy asked if it was some fashion thing. Kalyani, who sits behind me in Bengali class, said, "My uncle wears one to pray, my cousin wears one because his mother insists, and I know a boy who just likes it." She looked at me. "Which are you?" I realised I had no clean answer. Ma wants me to keep it on. Dadu says it has to do with learning, and I like feeling close to him. Some days I tuck it under my shirt, some days I don't. I'm still working it out. - Arnab

qa.q: Where did the boy ask Arnab about the thread?
qa.a: He asked in the changing room before PE.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel when Kalyani asked which he was?
qa.a: He felt uncertain, since he had no clean answer; his reasons seem to mix his mother's wish, closeness to Dadu and his own feeling.

qa.q: How could Arnab reply when someone asks what his thread means?
qa.a: He could share what he knows or say he is still working it out, without needing a tidy answer.

qa.q: What does Kalyani's list of people show?
qa.a: It shows that the same thread can be prayer, family insistence or personal taste, so nobody should assume what it means for someone else.

grounding: A teen wears a sacred thread whose meaning mixes faith, family expectation and choice, and nobody can assume it.

passage:
"Tenzin, what happened to your hair?" Binita stood in the bathroom doorway with a towel over her arm.
"It's just a streak, Ama. Blue. Like the prayer flags."
"Blue. Right." Binita came closer. "Did someone dare you?"
"No! My friends did theirs first, but I chose the colour myself. It washes out in a few weeks."
"And if the teacher says something?"
"Then I'll say it's temporary." Tenzin turned to the mirror. "Do you hate it?"
Binita tilted her head. "I'm surprised. Give me a minute." She touched the tip of the streak. "It's actually kind of nice with your eyes."
"Really?" Tenzin was already smiling.

qa.q: What colour is the streak in Tenzin's hair?
qa.a: The streak is blue, like the prayer flags.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling as she looks at the streak?
qa.a: Surprise first, and perhaps some worry about school, but her curiosity and the way she touches the streak suggest she is warming to it.

qa.q: How could Binita respond so that Tenzin keeps talking to her?
qa.a: She can stay curious, ask about the choice, and treat the streak as an experiment rather than a sign of trouble.

qa.q: Why might Tenzin ask 'Do you hate it?'
qa.a: Tenzin cares about Ama's opinion and is a little nervous, since a new look can feel like showing a new side of oneself.

grounding: A teen tries a new hair colour as trial and belonging, and a parent responds with curiosity, not alarm.

passage: I went through phases that year. First it was black eyeliner and my brother's old hoodies. Then thrifted shirts two sizes too big, and a tiny silver stud in my nose that Mummy allowed after a long discussion. Gurpreet, my best friend since Class 6, said, "You look different every week." She didn't say it unkindly, but I got defensive. "I'm trying things," I told her. And that was really it. I wasn't sad or hiding. I was checking which version felt like me, and which one my new friends in the art club liked. Most of it has gone now. The stud stayed. - Madhuri

qa.q: What small piece of jewellery did Madhuri get?
qa.a: She got a tiny silver stud in her nose.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel defensive when Gurpreet spoke?
qa.a: She may have heard judgement in the remark, even though Gurpreet did not say it unkindly; Madhuri was in the middle of trying things and didn't want them dismissed.

qa.q: How could a friend respond to someone changing style often?
qa.a: Stay curious and supportive, ask what they like about each look, and treat it as exploring rather than as a problem.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt watching her friend change so often?
qa.a: She may have been surprised or a little unsure of what to expect, but her remark did not sound unkind, so she probably was simply noticing.

grounding: A teen tries on styles and identities as trial and belonging, not as proof of deeper trouble.

passage: "When I was sixteen, Pranav, I wore a yellow scarf to every home match," Ishita said, stirring the tea. "I loved it. Thousands of us singing the same song, and my chest felt too big for my body. One afternoon the crowd behind us started pushing, and someone began chanting nasty things about the other team's supporters. I noticed I was chanting too, without thinking. That frightened me a little." She smiled at her grandson. "My friend Leela grabbed my sleeve, and we left through the side gate before the end. We heard the last overs on a shopkeeper's radio." "Did you regret missing it?" Pranav asked. "Not for a second. The scarf is still in the cupboard."

qa.q: What did Ishita wear to every home match when she was sixteen?
qa.a: She wore a yellow scarf to every home match.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she noticed she was chanting too?
qa.a: She felt a little frightened at how easily she had joined in without thinking, even though she also loved the belonging.

qa.q: What could a young person do when a crowd starts to turn unsafe?
qa.a: Notice the shift, stay with a trusted friend and leave calmly, as Ishita and Leela did through the side gate.

qa.q: How might Pranav see the story differently from Ishita?
qa.a: He may be surprised that his grandmother left a match she loved, and he might learn that belonging can be enjoyed while still using one's own judgement.

grounding: A teen loves crowd belonging but notices how a crowd amplifies pressure and chooses to leave when it turns unsafe.

passage: Rain hammered the stadium roof, and Kamal's blue-and-white face paint was running down his neck. He didn't care. Around him the whole stand bounced and sang, and for once he felt part of something huge. Rukmini, beside him, shouted in his ear that the exits were getting crowded. Then a group at the front began hurling insults at the away fans and the pushing started. Kamal caught himself joining the chant, his voice louder than he'd ever use alone, and it felt exciting and wrong at once. "Kamal!" Rukmini pulled his sleeve. "Come on." He looked at the singing crowd, then at her, and turned toward the stairs, still humming the tune.

qa.q: What was running down Kamal's neck?
qa.a: His blue-and-white face paint was running down his neck in the rain.

qa.q: How can you tell that Kamal feels mixed emotions about the crowd?
qa.a: He enjoys belonging, yet catches himself chanting louder than he would alone and feels it is exciting and wrong at once, then leaves while still humming.

qa.q: What would you advise Kamal and Rukmini to do if the pushing gets worse?
qa.a: Leave together by a clear exit and stay with each other, since belonging can be enjoyed without staying in a crowd that turns unsafe.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini to see Kamal join the chant?
qa.a: She may feel worried because he seems different from himself in the crowd, so she pulls his sleeve to bring him back.

grounding: A teen cheers with a crowd, feels belonging and amplified emotion, and wise judgement means leaving when it turns unsafe.

passage: Tarun, you asked what the vigil was like. I'm Nilesh, by the way, Class 10. Honestly, it was quieter than I expected. The whole school stood on the field with small lamps, and the boy we were remembering was a year below me, so I hardly knew him. Girls near me were crying. Somebody's little sister had brought marigolds. I kept waiting to feel something big. Mostly I felt strange and a bit numb, and then guilty about being numb. When the bell rang once for silence, my eyes suddenly stung, and I don't know why. Afterwards my friend Kabir said he'd felt nothing all evening and cried on the bus. I think people carry it differently. I just held my lamp very still.

qa.q: What did the girls near Nilesh do at the vigil?
qa.a: Girls near him were crying, and somebody's little sister had brought marigolds.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling before the bell rang?
qa.a: Mostly numb and strange, followed by guilt about being numb; his stinging eyes at the bell show that feelings can arrive unexpectedly.

qa.q: How could someone support a friend who feels numb at a memorial?
qa.a: Tell them that people carry grief differently and that no reaction is wrong, and listen if they want to talk later.

qa.q: How might Kabir's evening help Nilesh understand his own?
qa.a: Kabir felt nothing all evening and cried later, which shows that numbness and tears can both belong to the same grief.

grounding: A teen at a school vigil shows solidarity in silence and lamps while feeling numb, unlike others who cry.

passage: I stood two rows behind Vishal at the school memorial, so I saw more than I meant to. He carried the flowers up at the start, laid them very neatly, and then stayed at the edge of the group with his hands in his pockets. Girls around him were sobbing. Vishal never cried, not once, and he didn't look at anyone. Some of our class whispered that he didn't care. I don't think that's true, though I can't say what it was. When the lamps were lit, he stayed until the very last person had gone and straightened one of the candles before he left. I still don't know if that was grief, or just needing something to do. - Rajni

qa.q: What did Vishal do at the start of the memorial?
qa.a: He carried the flowers up and laid them very neatly.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling, and what is another possibility?
qa.a: He may have been grieving quietly, shown by staying till the end and straightening a candle; another possibility is that he felt numb and needed something to do.

qa.q: What could a classmate do rather than whisper that Vishal didn't care?
qa.a: They could remember that people show grief in different ways, and offer him a kind word or company without judging his reaction.

qa.q: How might the whispering feel to Vishal if he heard it?
qa.a: It could hurt, since he may be carrying feelings he cannot show, and being called uncaring would add to his burden. 🤍

grounding: A teen joins a school memorial where some cry and others, like Vishal, show grief differently or not visibly.

subtype: Affectionate and tender among friends and family [Regulating]
passage: "I'll tell you about my father, Keerthana," Ayesha said, patting the sofa. "When I was fifteen, he came to my school gate every day with my lunch and always tried to hug me. I hated it. Not him, the audience. So I'd wave from a distance and walk in fast. My friends thought I was cold." She laughed softly. "But at home I kept every note he tucked in the tiffin. One said, 'Eat properly, my clever girl.' I still have it." Keerthana looked at her. "Did you ever tell him?" "Years later. He said he'd known. Feelings don't always need a public stage, but they do need somewhere."

qa.q: Where did Ayesha's father come each day when she was fifteen?
qa.a: He came to her school gate every day with her lunch.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha wave from a distance and walk in fast?
qa.a: She was embarrassed by the audience, not by her father; she wanted to avoid a public hug while still loving him.

qa.q: What could Keerthana take from the story if she feels shy about affection?
qa.a: She could find a private way to show warmth, such as a note or a few honest words, so the bond stays alive.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's father have felt at the school gate?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit hurt or puzzled by the quick wave, though he says he knew she cared, so he probably understood.

grounding: A teen hides affection in public but stays warm privately through small notes.

subtype: Affectionate and tender among friends and family [Regulating]
passage: The school bell was due in three minutes when Hansa spotted her mother, Arohi, hurrying up the road with the forgotten lunch box held high. Her friends were right there. Hansa's stomach dropped. She walked to the gate, took the box, and said only, "Thanks, Ma. Go, go." Arohi wanted a hug, but she saw the group and simply squeezed Hansa's arm. In the classroom Hansa opened her bag and found a folded note on top of the lunch: "Do well today." She pressed her lips together to keep from smiling. At the break she sent a message from the corridor: "sorry I was rude. love you 🤍".

qa.q: What had Hansa forgotten at home?
qa.a: Hansa had forgotten her lunch box, which Arohi brought to the gate.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling at the gate and later at the break?
qa.a: At the gate she was embarrassed in front of her friends, and later she felt warm and a little guilty, which is why she sent her message. 🤍

qa.q: What small step could Hansa take so that her mother feels appreciated?
qa.a: She could keep sending a private message or thank her mother at home, so affection stays visible even when public hugs feel awkward.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel after the gate?
qa.a: She may feel a small sting at the rushed goodbye, but seeing the group she chose a squeeze of the arm, and the message afterwards will likely warm her.

grounding: A teen hides affection in front of friends but stays warm privately through a message.

passage: My friend Binita and I have joked about everything since Class 8. She calls me Mr Sleepy, I call her Wrong Turn because she gets lost in her own house. It's ours, and I love it. Last week in the canteen I posted a meme of her mixing up two buses and put it in the class chat. Twenty people reacted with 😂. Binita typed "haha" and nothing else. In person she was quiet and kept looking at her tray. I went cold, because she always sends me ten emojis back. I said sorry that evening. She told me she liked being teased by me, but not with an audience. I've learnt to watch her face, not just the reactions. - Tenzin

qa.q: Where did Tenzin post the meme about Binita?
qa.a: He put it in the class chat.

qa.q: What did Binita's short 'haha' and quiet mood suggest?
qa.a: Most likely she was hurt or embarrassed by the audience, since she usually sends many emojis; another possibility is that she was just tired.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do to keep the banter fun for both of them?
qa.a: Keep the jokes private, check Binita's response each time, and stop as soon as she seems uncomfortable.

qa.q: How might the twenty classmates' laughing reactions have felt to Binita?
qa.a: It may have felt like being laughed at by a crowd instead of joking with a close friend, even if each classmate meant no harm.

grounding: Banter signals closeness, but teasing hurts when one person isn't enjoying it; watching the response is the guide.

passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. During the group task I overheard Madhav calling Shankar "Professor Snail" because he takes time on his answers. The other boys laughed, and Madhav grinned at Shankar as he'd do with a friend. Shankar smiled thinly, then stopped writing and moved his chair a little away. He hadn't said anything, but he didn't contribute again that period. The two sit together at lunch, so I suspect Madhav means no harm, and I can't be sure how Shankar felt. I asked Shankar quietly afterwards whether he was fine with the nickname. He said he wasn't sure. Next I'll talk with Madhav about watching the other person's reaction, and check in with Shankar again.

qa.q: What nickname did Madhav use for Shankar?
qa.a: Madhav called him Professor Snail because he takes time on his answers.

qa.q: What did Shankar's thin smile and moving away suggest?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable, and possibly hurt, though the teacher can't be sure; another reading is that he was simply concentrating.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Madhav?
qa.a: Explain that banter works when both people enjoy it, and that Shankar's reaction is the guide to when it should stop.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the nickname differently from Shankar?
qa.a: Madhav probably thinks it is friendly play like their usual jokes at lunch, while Shankar may feel laughed at in front of the other boys.

grounding: Banter and nicknames signal closeness but hurt when one person doesn't enjoy the teasing; the reaction guides when to stop.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage:
Day one. Results were out at noon. Farida read her marks on the school portal, closed the laptop and said nothing at lunch. Her mother, Nandini, noticed she left her rice untouched.
Day four. Farida snapped at her younger brother over a borrowed pen, then muttered, "Don't bother with me, I'm useless. Everyone got more." Nandini stopped her chopping. She didn't lecture about studying harder or list other children's scores. She simply sat down by Farida and said, "That sounds heavy. Tell me more."
Day nine. Farida was still quiet and still saying she'd never be good at anything. Nandini called the school counsellor that morning and booked a time, and sat beside Farida while they spoke.

qa.q: What did Farida leave untouched at lunch on day one?
qa.a: She left her rice untouched.

qa.q: What might Farida be feeling when she says 'I'm useless'?
qa.a: She is probably deeply disappointed and hopeless, comparing herself with others; snapping at her brother may show the hurt spilling over.

qa.q: Why did Nandini contact the school counsellor on day nine?
qa.a: Because Farida stayed quiet and kept saying she'd never be good at anything, so the hopeless feeling wasn't fading and needed caring, professional attention.

qa.q: How might Farida experience her mother's choice not to lecture?
qa.a: She may feel listened to and less alone, whereas a lecture would likely have added to her sense of failure.

grounding: A teen after poor results goes silent, snaps and calls herself useless; the family responds with caring attention, not lectures.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage: "I was your age when I failed my second-year exams, Avni," said Jomon, turning the pages of an old photo album on the verandah. "I told everyone I was useless and stopped speaking at meals. My friends' results were all better, and I couldn't stand the comparison." He tapped a photograph of a stern man. "Your great-grandfather wanted to shout, I could see it. Instead he sat next to me on this bench every evening and said nothing for a week. Then he asked what I was afraid of. I told him." Jomon closed the album. "If you ever feel that heavy, come to me. Don't sit alone with it."

qa.q: Where did Jomon's father sit with him every evening?
qa.a: He sat next to Jomon on the bench on the verandah every evening.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling after failing his exams?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, shown by calling himself useless, stopping speaking at meals and being unable to bear the comparison with friends.

qa.q: What could Avni do if she ever feels that heavy?
qa.a: She could go to Jomon or another trusted adult and say what she's afraid of, instead of sitting alone with it.

qa.q: How might Jomon's father have felt as he sat silently?
qa.a: He probably wanted to shout or fix things, but he chose to stay close and wait, showing worry and care.

grounding: A teen after poor exam results says they are useless; caring attention from family, not lectures, helps.
